label: A Self is bounded by a cognitive light cone of events it can measure and affect
claim: Any Self (agent) is demarcated by a computational surface, the spatio-temporal boundary of the events it can measure, model and try to affect; this surface is a cognitive "light cone" that sets the scale and limits of its cognition and allows agents of very different material make-up to be compared.
quote: Any Self is demarcated by a computational surface – the spatio-temporal boundary of events that it can measure, model, and try to affect. This surface sets a functional boundary - a cognitive “light cone” which defines the scale and limits of its cognition.
scope: All agents: biological, artificial and exobiological
candidate_data: none known

label: An Individual is defined by the scale and types of goals it can pursue
claim: The scale and types of goals (in the cybernetic sense of feedback toward a specific state) that a system can pursue define the boundaries and content of that system as an agent or Individual; the coherent Self is the set of parts that operate together toward specific goal states.
quote: I propose a definition of an Individual based on its information-processing structure (Barandiaran et al., 2009): the scale and types of goals that a system can pursue defines (determines) the boundaries and content of the putative “agent.”
scope: Biological individuals at any level of organization, plus artificial and exobiological agents
candidate_data: none known

label: Most biological systems consist of multiple nested selves
claim: Under Scale-Free Cognition, most biological systems consist of multiple, nested selves rather than one, each inner agent maintaining its own Self only to the extent that it restricts information flow from its neighbours.
quote: It is an essential aspect of Scale-Free Cognition that most biological systems consist of multiple, nested selves [not one, as implied by Integrated Information Theory (Tononi, 2008)].
scope: Multilevel biological systems (molecular networks, cells, tissues, organs, organisms, swarms)
candidate_data: none known

label: Brain cognition lies on a continuum with conserved pre-neural computation
claim: Given the deep evolutionary conservation of ion-channel and neurotransmitter mechanisms between developmental and behavioural processes, the cognitive capacities of advanced brains are likely on a continuum with, and evolved from, much simpler computational processes conserved at both the functional and molecular levels.
quote: Thus, it is likely that the cognitive capacities of advanced brains lie on a continuum with, and evolve from, much simpler computational processes that are widely conserved at both the functional and mechanism (molecular) levels.
scope: Nervous systems and their pre-neural cellular precursors across the tree of life
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distribution of ion channel and neurotransmitter pathway genes
presence of learning or memory behaviours in aneural organisms
candidate_data: Comparative genomics and protein-family resources (UniProt, InterPro, OrthoDB) for ion channel and neurotransmitter gene distribution, plus published basal-cognition behavioural assays.

label: Somatic cells kept their computational capacities and scaled them to anatomical goals
claim: Somatic cells did not lose the behavioural plasticity and computational capabilities of their unicellular ancestors when they became part of metazoan bodies; they scaled them to pursue larger goals, namely building and maintaining complex anatomies.
quote: somatic cells did not lose their behavioral plasticity and computational capabilities in becoming part of metazoan swarms (bodies): they scaled them to enable pursuit of larger goals consisting of creation and upkeep of massively complex anatomies (Pezzulo and Levin, 2015).
scope: Metazoan somatic cells compared with unicellular ancestors
measurable_quantities: behavioural repertoire of isolated somatic cells
conservation of unicellular signalling and motility genes in metazoan somatic cells
candidate_data: Comparative genomics of unicellular holozoans and metazoans (e.g. Ensembl, UniProt) and single-cell motility and behaviour imaging datasets.

label: Cell collectives pursue organ-level target morphologies despite perturbation
claim: Regulative development and regeneration (e.g. scrambled tadpole faces that still become normal frog faces, tail grafts remodelling into limbs, kidney tubules of constant diameter despite enlarged cells) show that somatic cells pursue specific target morphologies despite perturbation, with set points that are large organ-level macrostates not defined at the single-cell level.
quote: They reveal the ability of somatic cells to not only pursue specific target morphologies despite perturbations and novel scenarios, but to pursue collective patterning outcomes that are truly enormous with respect to the scale of size and organization of single cells
scope: Regulative development and regeneration in vertebrates (Xenopus, salamanders, axolotls, newts)
measurable_quantities: final craniofacial configuration after organ displacement
regenerate size and pattern after amputation at different levels
tubule diameter versus cell size
candidate_data: Published Xenopus craniofacial rearrangement and regeneration image datasets (e.g. Xenbase, the Image Data Resource) and axolotl regeneration data.

label: Cell domains make coordinated group decisions, even random ones
claim: Cells join into domains that make decisions as a single unit: when left-right asymmetry is randomized in early embryos, a whole domain picks L or R identity rather than individual cells choosing independently, and in frog melanoma-like conversion all melanocytes in a body convert or not together.
quote: Remarkably, however, this randomization is made on a group level – in each case, the entire domain randomly picks L or R identity, not exhibiting a speckled appearance where each cell adopts a stochastic outcome. The decision is random, but all of the cells in the domain are coordinated to make the same random decision (Levin et al., 2002).
scope: Left-right patterning in early vertebrate embryos; melanocyte conversion in Xenopus tadpoles
measurable_quantities: spatial pattern of left- or right-specific gene expression after randomizing treatments
fraction of melanocytes converted per animal
candidate_data: Published left-right asymmetry in situ hybridization datasets and Xenopus melanocyte conversion image data (e.g. Xenbase).

label: Neural motor control may be an exaptation of bioelectric navigation of morphospace
claim: Neural control of body movement in three-dimensional space may be an evolutionary exaptation and speed-up of an older, slower role of bioelectric signalling: moving the body's configuration through anatomical morphospace during embryogenesis, repair and remodelling.
quote: Neural networks control the movement of a body in three-dimensional space; this scheme may be an evolutionary exaptation and speed-optimization of a more ancient, slower role of bioelectrical signaling: the movement of body configuration through anatomical morphospace during embryogenesis, repair, and remodeling (Sullivan et al., 2016; Mathews and Levin, 2018; Mclaughlin and Levin, 2018).
scope: Evolution of nervous systems from developmental bioelectric signalling in animals
measurable_quantities: shared ion channel and gap junction genes between developmental and neural bioelectric networks
phylogenetic order of appearance of developmental versus neural uses
candidate_data: Comparative genomics of ion channels and innexins/connexins across early-branching animals (UniProt, InterPro) and developmental expression atlases.

label: Cancer is a reversible shrinking of a cell's computational boundary
claim: Cancer is a reversible shrinking of the computational boundary of the Self: by becoming isolated from surrounding tissue's physiological (bioelectric) signals, a cell's cognitive boundary shrinks to its pre-multicellular, single-cell size, so it reverts to proliferating and migrating for its own benefit.
quote: Cancer is a (reversible) shrinking of the computational boundary of a biosystem: by isolating itself from the surrounding tissue’s physiological signals, a cell’s cognitive boundary shrinks to the small size it had before multicellularity.
scope: Carcinogenic transformation in metazoan tissues
measurable_quantities: gap junctional coupling between tumour cells and neighbours
resting membrane potential of transformed versus normal cells
tumour incidence after restoring coupling
candidate_data: Cancer transcriptomic and expression data for gap junction and ion channel genes (e.g. The Cancer Genome Atlas, the Gene Expression Omnibus) and published Xenopus tumour bioelectric experiments.

label: Cancer cells are no more selfish than normal cells; their self is smaller
claim: Cells in a metazoan body are not less selfish than unicellular organisms or cancer cells; all are equally selfish, but the self that normal somatic cells defend is larger in space, time and complexity, its boundary being set by how far information passes between subunits.
quote: They are equally selfish, working only for the benefit of themselves, but the relevant self that they defend is bigger in terms of space, time, and complexity. As will be argued below, what defines this Self is the boundary of information being able to pass between the subunits.
scope: Somatic metazoan cells, cancer cells and unicellular organisms
candidate_data: none known

label: Disrupting or restoring cell communication should trigger or suppress cancer
claim: The shrinking-Self view of cancer predicts that interfering with physiological communication among cells should be able to trigger cancer and restoring it should suppress cancer, and that the relevant parameter (communication) is spread over considerable distance rather than confined to single cells as genomic damage is.
quote: This view predicts that interference with (or restoration of) physiological communication among cells should be able to trigger (or suppress) cancer and that the relevant parameter (communication) is spread out over considerable distance and not confined to single cells (e.g., genomic damage).
scope: Metazoan tissues; tested so far in amphibian models
measurable_quantities: tumour incidence after gap junction blockade
tumour incidence after restoring coupling or membrane potential
spatial range of the cells whose state affects tumour formation
candidate_data: Published Xenopus tumour and depolarization experiments, carcinogenicity data on gap junction blockers, and cancer expression data in the Gene Expression Omnibus.

label: Depolarization induces and hyperpolarization prevents tumour-like changes in tadpoles
claim: In tadpoles, depolarizing a specific cell population is sufficient to cause metastatic-like transformation of normal melanocytes in genetically normal animals, while optogenetic or constitutive hyperpolarization prevents human oncogenes from inducing tumours.
quote: metastatic transformation of normal melanocytes can be achieved in genetically normal tadpoles simply by depolarizing a specific cell population (Lobikin et al., 2012), while, conversely, human oncogenes which normally induce tumors can be prevented from doing so simply by optogenetic or constitutive hyperpolarization (Chernet and Levin, 2013b, 2014; Chernet et al., 2015, 2016).
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles; melanocytes and human-oncogene-induced tumours
measurable_quantities: resting membrane potential of target cells
fraction of animals with melanocyte hyperpigmentation and invasion
tumour incidence with and without hyperpolarization
candidate_data: The cited Levin-lab Xenopus studies' published counts and imaging; Xenbase for gene and reagent information.

label: Cognitive light cones have expanded over evolutionary time
claim: The volume of possible cognitive light cones (spatio-temporal boundaries of agents' goals) has presumably kept expanding over evolutionary time, through innovations in body structure that drastically enlarge the cognitive boundary, although some lineages contract it permanently or in particular life stages.
quote: Presumably, the volume of possible cognitive light cones keeps expanding with evolutionary time (although some lineages can contract it, permanently or during specific ontogenetic life stages). Over evolutionary scales, there have been “inflationary leaps” – innovations in body structure which drastically increase the cognitive boundary of viable selves.
scope: Evolution of agents across the tree of life
measurable_quantities: estimated spatial and temporal range of sensing, memory and anticipation per lineage over geological time
candidate_data: Comparative behavioural and memory-span data across taxa combined with dated phylogenies (e.g. TimeTree); no dataset directly measures cognitive light cones.

label: Agents scaled up from homeostatic loops by adding memory, anticipation and networks
claim: Agents evolved by scaling up from basic homeostatic loops (whose set points are the first goals), driven by surprise minimization, through the successive addition of delays (memory), anticipation (inference), and spatially distributed networks that allow learning and abstraction.
quote: Agents scaled up by evolving from basic homeostatic loops, driven by active inference (surprise minimization) via addition of delays (memory), anticipation (inference), and networks (spatially-distributed processing that enables learning and progressive abstraction/generalization from data).
scope: Evolution of agency from early living systems to complex organisms
measurable_quantities: presence of memory and anticipatory signalling circuits in unicellular lineages
phylogenetic ordering of homeostatic, anticipatory and networked control
candidate_data: Systems-biology model repositories (BioModels) of bacterial chemotaxis and anticipatory circuits, plus comparative genomics; no direct dataset for the full sequence.

label: Memory and learning are the origin of developmental modularity
claim: Memory can be the beginning of modularity because learning compresses complex states into simple triggers; in somatic control networks this appears as developmental modules in which a single simple driver (e.g. a bioelectric state) initiates a complex morphogenetic cascade such as building an eye or hand.
quote: Importantly, memory can serve as the beginning of modularity because learning essentially groups diverse stimuli into compressed representations: complex states of affairs become remembered as compact biophysical engrams – this is the essence of the kind of modularity when a simple biophysical event kicks off the formation of a complex morphogenetic cascade such as building a “hand” in embryogenesis.
scope: Developmental control networks in animals
measurable_quantities: information content of a triggering signal versus the organ it induces
frequency of single-trigger induction of whole organs (e.g. ectopic eyes)
candidate_data: Published ectopic-organ induction experiments in Xenopus (e.g. bioelectric eye induction) and developmental gene-network models in BioModels.

label: Animal senses use the same ion channel mechanisms found in bacteria
claim: The senses of complex animals (touch, taste, temperature, hearing, etc.) are mediated by the same ion channel mechanisms that bacteria already used to sense their world.
quote: Complex animals’ sense of touch, taste, temperature, hearing, etc. are mediated by the exact same ion channel mechanisms that were already discovered by bacteria and used to make sense of their world (Tasneem et al., 2005; Blackwell, 2006; Liebeskind et al., 2012; Nilius and Honore, 2012).
scope: Sensory ion channels in animals and their bacterial homologues
measurable_quantities: homology of animal sensory channels (mechanosensitive, thermosensitive, voltage-gated) to bacterial channel families
candidate_data: Protein family and phylogeny resources (InterPro, Pfam, UniProt) and structural data in the Protein Data Bank.

label: Cells in development minimize surprise and variational free energy like nervous systems
claim: Living systems minimize surprise and optimize variational free energy by tuning internal states to best predict future stimuli, and this holds for individual cells during metazoan development as much as for nervous systems.
quote: Systems minimize surprise and optimize variational free energy by tuning their internal states in a way that optimally predicts future stimuli (Friston and Ao, 2012; Friston, 2013; Badcock et al., 2019). This is as true for nervous systems as it is for individual cells during metazoan development (Friston et al., 2015; Ramstead et al., 2019).
scope: Nervous systems and individual cells in metazoan development
measurable_quantities: fit of active-inference models to cell signalling and migration time series
prediction error of cellular responses to repeated stimuli
candidate_data: Time-lapse cell signalling and morphogenesis datasets (e.g. the Image Data Resource, Cell Image Library) for fitting free-energy models.

label: Multicellularity and morphological complexity are driven by greedy infotaxis
claim: Morphological complexity and multicellularity are proposed to be driven by greedy infotaxis: cells collecting as much information as possible from as far away in space and time as possible to minimize surprise, with greater network connectivity enlarging what the compound individual can sense, remember and store.
quote: It is proposed that morphological complexity and multicellularity are driven by greedy infotaxis (Vergassola et al., 2007) – collecting as much information as possible, from as far away (in both space and time) as possible, to minimize surprise and optimize prediction.
scope: Origin of multicellularity and morphological complexity
measurable_quantities: information gain of cells in connected versus isolated states
outcomes of simulated or experimental evolution of multicellularity under information-seeking selection
candidate_data: Experimental-evolution studies of multicellularity (e.g. snowflake yeast, Chlamydomonas) and agent-based simulations; no dataset directly tests infotaxis as the driver.

label: Gap-junction coupling lets cells share sensing and form a larger Self
claim: When cells are coupled into networks by gap junctions, the whole collective can measure and act on the same sensory data, so its Umwelt expands into a larger individual; physiological connectivity is thus the binding mechanism for larger unified Selves.
quote: When coupled into networks via gap junctions however, the whole collective can measure and act upon the same sensory data – the Umwelt expands to create a larger individual in which the comprising cells share a unifying picture of the world (Figure 4).
scope: Gap-junction-coupled cell networks in animal tissues
measurable_quantities: spread of a local stimulus response across coupled versus uncoupled tissue
pattern-level outcomes after gap junction blockade
candidate_data: Published gap junction blocker patterning experiments (e.g. planarian and Xenopus studies), and connexin/innexin expression in Xenbase or PlanMine.

label: Most anesthetics in plants and animals are gap junction uncouplers
claim: Most anesthetics that remove cognition and sensory experience, in both plants and animals, act as gap junctional (bioelectric) uncouplers, which the author takes as consistent with connectivity binding cells into larger Selves.
quote: It is thus no coincidence that most anesthetics used to remove cognition and sensory experience, whether in plants or animals, are gap junctional (bioelectric) uncouplers (Mantz et al., 1993; Wentlandt et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2012; Gremiaux et al., 2014; Baluska et al., 2016).
scope: General and volatile anesthetics used in plants and animals
measurable_quantities: fraction of anesthetics that inhibit gap junction conductance at clinical concentrations
candidate_data: Pharmacology databases (ChEMBL, DrugBank, IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology) for anesthetic targets and gap junction activity.

label: Swarms should show the same cognitive illusions as vertebrate brains
claim: The proposed scale-invariant scaling of cognition predicts that swarm organisms should fall prey to the same kinds of cognitive illusions and failures of rationality as vertebrate brains, which the author says has been observed in ants and slime molds.
quote: A prediction of this proposed scaling is that swarm organisms should fall prey to the same kinds of cognitive illusions and specific failures of rationality as do vertebrate brains, which has indeed been observed in ants and slime molds (Sakiyama and Gunji, 2013, 2016; Tani et al., 2014; Beekman and Latty, 2015).
scope: Swarm and collective organisms (ants, slime molds) compared with vertebrate brains
measurable_quantities: decoy and context effects in collective choice
susceptibility to visual-illusion analogues in Physarum or ant colonies
candidate_data: Published collective decision-making experiments on ants and Physarum, some deposited in Dryad.

label: Selves form only at intermediate levels of information sharing between subunits
claim: Cognitive light cones grow or shrink as an agent's organization changes, and the key is a balance of selective information sharing through "synapses" (any structures that gate signals based on the state of others): too little sharing fails to bind subunits into a new Self, and too much yields an undifferentiated soup without modules or layered abstraction.
quote: Too little sharing results in a failure to bind subunits into a new Self. Too much sharing results in a homogenous soup with insufficient differentiation of modules and abstraction of information across distinct layers.
scope: Multicellular and multi-agent biological systems
measurable_quantities: degree of gap junctional coupling
degree of tissue differentiation and modularity
coherence of collective behaviour
candidate_data: Network simulations of coupled cells and published gap junction gain- and loss-of-function patterning data; no dedicated dataset known.

label: Morphogenetic goal-directedness smooths the fitness landscape and boosts evolvability
claim: Morphogenetic goal-directedness is a major evolutionary ratchet: because tissues adjust to reach the same anatomical goals despite changed conditions (e.g. muscle, vessels and tendons building a workable extra finger around an ectopic bone), it hides the disruptive effects of random mutations and smooths the anatomical fitness landscape.
quote: Morphogenetic goal-directedness is a major evolutionary ratchet, smoothing the anatomical fitness landscape by hiding the otherwise potentially disruptive effects of random mutations.
scope: Evolution of anatomy in organisms with regulative development
measurable_quantities: phenotypic effect distribution of mutations with and without developmental compensation
evolutionary search speed in models with competent versus passive cells
candidate_data: Mutant phenotype databases (e.g. ZFIN, Xenbase, MGI) and evolutionary simulation studies; no dataset directly measures landscape smoothing.

label: Brains are not hardwired: ectopic tail eyes in tadpoles still support vision
claim: Brains, like other developing organs, are not hardwired but can ascertain the body's structure and adjust their programs; tadpoles made to develop eyes on their tails, connected to the spinal cord rather than the brain, can still see quite well.
quote: Tadpoles engineered to develop with eyes on their tails instead of in their usual spot can see quite well, despite the fact that the eyes connect to the spinal cord, not the brain (Blackiston and Levin, 2013; Blackiston et al., 2017). Brains, like other developing organs, are not hardwired but are able to ascertain the structure of the body and adjust their functional programs accordingly
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with ectopic eyes; developing nervous systems generally
measurable_quantities: visual learning performance of eyeless tadpoles with ectopic eyes
innervation path of ectopic eyes
candidate_data: The cited Blackiston and Levin behavioural datasets; Xenbase for anatomy and reagents.

label: Editing bioelectric pattern set points can reprogram anatomy without genome editing
claim: A better strategy for regenerative medicine than genetic rewiring of cells may be to edit the pattern-homeostatic set point and let wild-type cells build to it, as shown by altering bioelectric state in planaria to give permanently double-headed worms without genomic editing.
quote: I have previously suggested that a better strategy than cellular re-wiring at the genetic level may be to edit the pattern-homeostatic set point and let wild-type cells build to the new spec. For example, the ability to re-write target morphology in planarian regeneration was recently shown, by altering the bioelectric state in flatworms, without genomic editing, giving rise to permanently double-headed worms (Durant et al., 2017; Levin et al., 2018).
scope: Regenerative medicine; planarian regeneration as the demonstrating case
measurable_quantities: persistence of double-headed phenotype across rounds of amputation
bioelectric pattern before and after treatment
regenerative outcome of set-point editing versus genetic interventions
candidate_data: Published planarian double-head experiments and planarian genomic and expression resources (PlanMine, SmedGD).

label: Bioelectric circuits act as software: multistable states switched without genetic change
claim: Ion channel and gap junction circuits are well suited to the "software" of life because they form feedback loops that implement dynamical systems with multiple attractors, which transient signals can switch between without changing the hardware (i.e. without mutating the DNA encoding the channels).
quote: What makes electric circuits, whether ion channel-mediated or electronic, good for software is that they easily implement dynamical systems that have multiple attractors and can be made to occupy one physiological state or another by transient inputs (signals), not requiring changing the hardware (i.e., mutating the DNA encoding that hardware).
scope: Bioelectric networks of ion channels and gap junctions in cells and tissues
measurable_quantities: number of stable membrane-potential states in cell networks
persistence of a bioelectric state after a transient stimulus without transcriptional change
candidate_data: Published bioelectric network models (e.g. BETSE simulations, BioModels) and voltage-dye imaging of tissues.

label: Opiate addictiveness may derive from an ancient role in keeping cells together
claim: If multicellularity arose from a drive to minimize predictive error, cells need a way to keep other cells nearby; this suggests the testable hypothesis that the addictive power of opiates and similar molecules derives from such ancient roots, which could be tested in early models of multicellularity and stem/somatic cell co-cultures.
quote: Specifically, the implementation of multicellularity by the drive to minimize predictive error (Fields and Levin, 2019) suggests that cells need a way to keep other cells nearby. This suggests the testable hypothesis that the addictive power of opiates and similar molecules derives from such ancient roots.
scope: Opioid and addiction-related signalling in early multicellular models and cell co-cultures
measurable_quantities: effect of opioid agonists/antagonists on cell aggregation or co-culture cohesion
phylogenetic distribution of opioid-like signalling
candidate_data: Comparative genomics of opioid receptor families (InterPro, OrthoDB); new aggregation assays would be needed.

label: Forced electrogenic and gap junction expression could make unicells form bodies
claim: The proposed role of bioelectrics in multicellularity predicts that forcing expression of appropriate electrogenic proteins and gap junctions in a unicellular organism should induce metazoan-like bodies, and that appropriate changes of bioelectric dynamics may dissolve a metazoan body.
quote: The proposed crucial role of bioelectrics in multicellularity predicts that it should be possible to induce the formation of metazoan-like bodies in an otherwise unicellular organism by forcing the expression of appropriate electrogenic proteins and gap junctions. Similarly, it may be possible to induce dissolution of an entire metazoan body by appropriate changes of bioelectric dynamics.
scope: Unicellular organisms engineered with electrogenic proteins and gap junctions; metazoan bodies
measurable_quantities: formation of stable multicellular aggregates after transgene expression
coherence of a metazoan body after bioelectric perturbation
candidate_data: none known

label: Regeneration across kingdoms should consistently use electrogenic proteins
claim: Bioelectrics should be widely conserved in regeneration across kingdoms: transcriptomes of regeneration from damaged bacterial biofilms to plants to animal limb and organ regeneration should show consistent use of electrogenic proteins, and neurotransmitter signalling should be conserved enough that cognitive-modulator drugs affect biofilms and Physarum.
quote: Bioelectrics should be widely conserved in regeneration across Kingdoms; transcriptomic analyses of regeneration events from damaged bacterial biofilms to plants to metazoan models of limb and organ regeneration should all show consistent use of electrogenic proteins in the events that enable cooperation toward self-limiting morphogenetic cascades.
scope: Regeneration in bacterial biofilms, plants and animals
measurable_quantities: differential expression of ion channel, pump and gap junction genes during regeneration
effects of neuroactive drugs on biofilm and Physarum behaviour
candidate_data: Regeneration transcriptome series in the Gene Expression Omnibus and species resources such as PlanMine and Xenbase.

label: Cells and tissues may have something it is like to make decisions
claim: Because some nervous systems give rise to first-person experience and neural and non-neural networks differ minimally apart from time scale, it is natural to hypothesize that there is something it is like to be a tissue or organ making decisions, e.g. a pancreas may have as much proto-consciousness as a simple neural network.
quote: But, given that at least some nervous systems do give rise to such experience and that the differences between neural networks and non-neural ones (aside from temporal scale) are minimal, it is natural to hypothesize that there is something-it-is-like to being a tissue or organ and making decisions.
scope: Non-neural tissues and organs
candidate_data: none known

label: Evolutionary algorithms can design novel living organisms built from frog cells
claim: A pipeline in which an evolutionary algorithm designs candidate organisms in silico for a desired function, and transferable designs are then built from Xenopus cells with a cell-based construction toolkit, can produce novel living systems that show the predicted behaviours, though some steps still need manual intervention.
quote: Here we show a scalable pipeline for creating functional novel lifeforms: AI methods automatically design diverse candidate lifeforms in silico to perform some desired function, and transferable designs are then created using a cell-based construction toolkit to realize living systems with the predicted behaviors.
scope: Xenopus laevis embryonic epidermal and cardiac progenitor tissue shaped into designed aggregates
measurable_quantities: match between simulated and observed shape
match between simulated and observed locomotion
candidate_data: The paper's source code on GitHub (named in its Data Availability statement) and its SI movement tracks.

label: Shape concavities of 100 µm or more persist in developing stem cell aggregates
claim: Aggregates of developing Xenopus pluripotent cells tend to close small gaps in their geometry; concavities 100 µm wide or more (12% of body length) gave stable long-term deformations, setting the minimal buildable feature size.
quote: Preliminary work determined that concavities with a width of 100 µm or greater (12% of total body length) produced stable long-term deformations suitable for biological building (SI Appendix, Fig. S7).
scope: Reaggregated Xenopus laevis animal-cap tissue shaped by microsurgery
measurable_quantities: concavity width
persistence of concavity over the organism's lifespan
candidate_data: The paper's SI imaging; new shaping experiments in Xenopus.

label: Designed organisms moved as simulated when upright, much less when inverted
claim: For at least one deciliated, cardiac-muscle-powered design, the upright organisms' direction of movement matched that of the in silico design under random perturbations, and inverting the design significantly reduced net displacement both in silico and in vivo.
quote: More specifically, the upright organisms’ direction of movement matched that of the in silico design under random perturbations (P < 0.01; details in SI Appendix, section S9), and inverting the design significantly reduced its net displacement both in silico (P < 0.001) and in vivo (P < 0.0001).
scope: Deciliated Xenopus reconfigurable organisms with cardiac tissue, compared with their simulated designs
measurable_quantities: direction of movement
net displacement upright versus inverted
candidate_data: The paper's movement tracks (SI) and GitHub code; repeat tracking experiments.

label: Behaviour transfer from simulation to organism was due to the designed shape
claim: The authors interpret the orientation-dependent match between simulated and living organisms as showing that successful transfer of locomotion from simulation to the living organism was due to the designed morphology itself, not chance.
quote: This suggests that successful transference did not result by chance but rather was due to the design itself.
scope: Evolved designs realized as Xenopus reconfigurable organisms
measurable_quantities: locomotion of designed versus random or scrambled shapes built from the same tissues
candidate_data: The paper's SI movement data; control builds of non-evolved shapes would be needed.

label: Motile designs spontaneously aggregate particles in simulation and in vivo
claim: When the environment contains particulate matter, motile designs spontaneously gather the particles into aggregates, both in simulation and as living Xenopus-cell organisms.
quote: When the environment is strewn with particulate matter, motile designs spontaneously aggregate the external objects both in silico (SI Appendix, Fig. S10) and in vivo (Fig. 3F and SI Appendix, Fig. S11).
scope: Xenopus reconfigurable organisms and their simulated counterparts in a particle-strewn dish
measurable_quantities: particle cluster size and number over time
candidate_data: The paper's SI videos and GitHub simulation code.

label: Pairs of organisms collide, bond and orbit, more so with cilia active
claim: Collective behaviours predicted in simulation were observed in vivo: two organisms often collide, form a temporary mechanical bond and orbit each other for several revolutions before detaching, and this is more pronounced when cilia are not inhibited.
quote: For instance, two designs often collide, form a temporary mechanical bond, and orbit about each other for several revolutions before detaching along tangential trajectories (SI Appendix, Fig. S10). This phenomenon is more pronounced when cilia are not inhibited on the organisms
scope: Multiple Xenopus reconfigurable organisms sharing a dish, with and without cilia
measurable_quantities: frequency and duration of pairwise bonding and orbiting
effect of ciliation on entanglement
candidate_data: The paper's SI videos; new tracking experiments.

label: Selection for locomotion under random actuation evolved derandomizing shapes
claim: In the voxel-based soft-body simulation with randomly phased contractile cells, selection for locomotion produced morphologies that derandomize motion: shape and the distribution of passive and contractile cells evolved so the global movement was coherent despite random actuation.
quote: As a side effect of selection pressure for locomotion, derandomizing morphologies evolved: evolutionary improvement occurred through changes in overall shape, and distribution of the passive and contractile cells, to collectively derandomize the global movement produced by the random actuation.
scope: Evolutionary design in a soft-body physics simulation of passive and contractile voxels
measurable_quantities: net displacement under random phase offsets
morphological features of evolved designs
candidate_data: The paper's GitHub source code for rerunning the evolutionary simulations.

label: Cardiomyocytes in built organisms spontaneously made phase-matched contractions
claim: Although signalling between cardiomyocytes was not designed or enforced, cardiac muscle cells in the built organisms spontaneously coordinated to produce coherent, phase-matched contractions that aided locomotion.
quote: For instance, although signaling between cardiomyocytes was not enforced, emergent spontaneous coordination among the cardiac muscle cells produced coherent, phase-matched contractions which aided locomotion in the physically realized designs.
scope: Xenopus cardiac progenitor tissue embedded in reconfigurable organisms
measurable_quantities: phase relationship of contractions across the cardiac tissue
displacement per contraction cycle
candidate_data: The paper's SI videos; calcium or voltage imaging in new builds.

label: Reconfigurable organisms self-repair, closing lacerations
claim: Reconfigurable organisms built from Xenopus cells maintain their externally imposed shape and also self-repair after damage, for example automatically closing lacerations.
quote: Finally, reconfigurable organisms not only self-maintain their externally imposed configuration, but they also self-repair in the face of damage, such as automatically closing lacerations (SI Appendix, Fig. S9).
scope: Xenopus laevis reconfigurable organisms
measurable_quantities: time to wound closure
shape recovery after laceration
candidate_data: The paper's SI imaging; new wounding experiments.

label: Cell competence lets neural-less novel aggregates self-organize functionally
claim: The behavioural competence of individual cells and their propensity to cooperate in groups facilitate functional morphogenesis in novel circumstances, so that the designed organisms, despite lacking nervous systems, following novel developmental trajectories and mixing tissues, still possess self-organizing properties that support their designed behaviour.
quote: The behavioral competence of individual cells, and the propensity of cells to cooperate in groups, facilitate functional morphogenesis in novel circumstances. The lifeforms presented here, despite lacking nervous systems, following novel developmental trajectories, and being composed of materials from different tissues, nevertheless possess these self-organizing properties.
scope: Xenopus cells in novel, designed multicellular configurations

label: Adding hydrodynamics and random actuation made simulated gaits match living ones
claim: Designs first evolved on simulated land had bounding gaits that did not transfer to living organisms; adding first-order hydrodynamics and randomized phase offsets produced designs whose behaviour better matched the living systems, in contact with the ground for 93.3% of evaluation versus 52.7% on the first pass.
quote: The behavior of designs generated on the second pass better matched the behavior of the actual living systems: on average, designs were in contact with the ground plane for 93.3% of their evaluation period, compared to just 52.7% on the first pass (SI Appendix, section S6).
